name: Depth / dimensionality
controls: How much spatial depth the graphic world has and how it is constructed: a single flat plane, flat layers separated in depth, flat drawings that imply volume, or real three-dimensional geometry seen through a camera.
question: How flat or deep should the world feel?
notes: Four levels, often confused. 2D: everything lives on one picture plane; motion is x/y translation, rotation around the axis facing the viewer, and scale used as a graphic change (not as approach). 2.5D: flat 2D layers (cards, cutouts, UI panels) placed at different distances along z and viewed through a perspective camera, so parallax and perspective emerge from real depth, but every layer stays a flat card that never shows a side; this is the multiplane-camera principle and After Effects 3D layers, and in the browser it is CSS perspective plus translateZ. Pseudo-3D: flat drawings or flat elements that imply volume through drawn or computed cues (extrusion, shading, isometric projection, a card flip with rotateY) without a real 3D model; the illusion only holds from the angles the artist prepared, and turning the object further breaks it. True 3D: geometry with volume, lit and rendered by a virtual camera, valid from any angle; it needs WebGL (Three.js) or pre-rendered footage. Usage varies: many designers say 2.5D and pseudo-3D interchangeably, and 'isometric' is often used for any axonometric projection. Projection (isometric, orthographic, perspective) is a separate axis from construction (flat, layered, modeled): an isometric scene can be drawn flat (pseudo-3D) or rendered from real models with an orthographic camera (orthographic 3D). Depth choice constrains camera: a dolly or orbit is only meaningful in 2.5D and 3D. Depth cues that sell any level: overlap, relative scale, atmospheric perspective (distant layers lighter and less saturated), depth of field, cast shadows and parallax.

options.what: Depth read only from which element covers which and how large they are.
options.prompt: Establish depth with overlap and relative scale only: nearer elements are larger and cover farther ones; no blur, shadow or tonal change.

options.what: Distant layers are lighter, lower in contrast and less saturated, as if seen through air.
options.prompt: Apply atmospheric perspective: each step back in depth raises lightness 8-12%, lowers saturation 15-20% and reduces contrast toward the background color; the nearest layer keeps full contrast.

options.what: Layers away from the focal plane are blurred in proportion to their distance.
options.prompt: Blur layers by distance from the focal plane: filter: blur() of 0 at focus, 2-4px one step away, 6-10px two steps away; keep text only on in-focus layers.

options.what: Shadows show how far elements float above the ground or each other.
options.prompt: Show height with cast shadows: shadow offset and blur grow with elevation (2px/4px blur at rest, 16px/32px blur when lifted) while shadow opacity drops from 20% to 10%.

options.what: Everything on one picture plane with no depth cues at all: no overlap hierarchy, shadow, perspective or parallax.
options.looks: Graphic shapes, type and UI laid out like a poster; flat fills; the frame reads as a surface, not a space.
options.motion: Translation in x/y, rotation around the viewing axis, scale as a graphic transformation, morphs and masks; camera, if any, is a flat pan or scale of the whole plane.
options.use: Kinetic typography, Swiss and minimalist motion, flat explainers, icon and logo animation, data visualization.
options.vs: Layered 2D uses overlap and z-order to separate planes; pure flat does not imply stacking. Perfectly flat (material) is about surface, not space.
options.prompt: Keep the world strictly flat: one picture plane, no drop shadows, perspective, parallax, depth blur or z-stacking cues. Motion is limited to x/y translation, rotation around the viewing axis, scale, masks and morphs. Any scale change reads as a graphic transformation, not an object approaching.

options.what: Flat elements stacked in a clear front-to-back order through overlap, subtle shadows or tone, but still on a flat picture plane.
options.looks: Cards on cards, cutout shapes overlapping, soft shadows separating layers; no perspective distortion.
options.motion: Layers slide over and under each other, lift with shadow growth, reorder in z; no parallax from a moving camera.
options.use: UI animation (cards, modals, stacks), paper-cutout styles, material-style product motion, illustrated explainers.
options.vs: 2.5D places layers at real distances so a moving camera produces parallax; layered 2D only stacks them visually. Parallax is a motion effect; layered 2D is a static construction.
options.prompt: Stack flat elements in explicit z-order (3-5 layers max) separated by overlap and soft shadows that grow with elevation; no perspective, no camera parallax. Changes in hierarchy are shown by elements lifting (2-4px translateY, shadow grows) and sliding over or under neighbors.

options.what: Flat 2D layers placed at different depths in a 3D space and viewed through a perspective camera, so movement produces real parallax and perspective.
options.looks: Flat cutouts, photos or UI panels spaced out in depth like theatre flats; near layers large and fast, far layers small and slow; layers never show their edges.
options.motion: Camera pushes, trucks and drifts through the layers; depth-of-field shifts between planes; layers can rotate slightly toward camera but never turn edge-on.
options.use: Photo animation and documentary graphics, illustrated brand films, UI-in-space product shots, title sequences.
options.conveys: Immersion and cinematic depth at 2D cost; storybook or diorama feeling.
options.vs: Pseudo-3D fakes volume within a single element; 2.5D has real spatial separation between flat elements. True 3D elements have volume and can be seen from any side.
options.prompt: Build the scene as 3-6 flat layers inside a container with perspective: 1200-1800px and transform-style: preserve-3d, each layer at a different translateZ (e.g. -800, -400, 0, 200px) and scaled up by (perspective - z) / perspective so it still fills the frame. Move the camera by animating the container (translateZ for push-in, translateX for truck) so parallax emerges naturally. Keep layer rotation under 25 degrees so no card turns edge-on.

options.what: Layers move at different speeds according to their implied distance, producing a sense of depth from motion alone.
options.looks: Foreground elements sweep past quickly, background drifts slowly; static frames can look flat, depth appears only in motion.
options.motion: Horizontal or vertical drifts with speed multipliers per layer (e.g. foreground 1.5x, mid 1x, background 0.3x); easing shared so layers stay coherent.
options.use: Landing-page heroes, photo animation, illustrated scenes, scrolling UI showcases, title cards.
options.conveys: Depth, smoothness, immersion; a sense of travel.
options.vs: 2.5D produces parallax from real z-depth and a perspective camera; plain parallax fakes it with 2D speed multipliers and no perspective. Parallax camera (camera dimension) is the move; parallax depth is the construction.
options.prompt: Separate the scene into 3-4 depth layers and move them with speed multipliers on the same tween: foreground 1.4-1.8x, subject 1x, midground 0.6x, background 0.2-0.3x of the camera travel. Same ease (power2.inOut or sine.inOut) for all layers. Scale foreground layers up 5-10% so their edges never enter frame.

options.what: Flat elements that imply volume through shading, perspective drawing or CSS 3D rotation of flat planes, without any real 3D model.
options.looks: Cards that flip and tilt in perspective, drawn objects with shading and highlights, faked perspective grids; convincing from chosen angles only.
options.motion: Card flips (rotateY), tilts toward the viewer, perspective skews, shading that shifts as an object turns; turns stay under the angle where the illusion breaks.
options.use: UI card flips and tilts, logo reveals, illustrated product motion, social content.
options.conveys: Dimensionality and polish without 3D production cost.
options.vs: 2.5D spaces flat layers apart in depth; pseudo-3D gives a single flat element the look of volume. Extruded 2D is a specific pseudo-3D technique (thickness added by stacking). Many designers use 2.5D and pseudo-3D interchangeably.
options.prompt: Imply volume on flat elements: use rotateX/rotateY with perspective: 1000px on individual cards (tilts of 8-20 degrees, flips of 180 degrees with backface-visibility: hidden), and shift a linear-gradient shading layer across the face in step with the rotation (lighter facing the light, 10-15% darker turning away). Never rotate a flat element past 70 degrees while its edge is visible.

options.what: Scale and placement exploited so objects look much nearer, farther, larger or smaller than they are, creating optical illusions.
options.looks: A tiny element aligned to look huge against a distant one, or a flat graphic that 'sits' on a surface in footage; illusions that resolve only from one viewpoint.
options.motion: The camera moves or the objects slide to reveal the trick (the illusion breaking is often the payoff), or elements are carefully held in alignment.
options.use: Playful brand films, surreal and conceptual motion, product films that play with scale, social content.
options.vs: Perspective 3D renders correct spatial relationships; forced perspective deliberately misleads them. Isometric has no vanishing points at all.
options.prompt: Stage a forced-perspective illusion: size and place a near element so it aligns exactly with a far element to read as one object (e.g. a small UI card 'resting' on a distant building). Hold the alignment for at least 1.5s, then reveal the trick by trucking the camera or sliding the near layer 15-25% sideways so the scale relationship breaks, over 800ms with power2.inOut.

options.what: A parallel projection in which the three axes are drawn at equal 120-degree angles, with no vanishing points or foreshortening.
options.looks: Diamond-grid scenes: objects drawn on 30-degree diagonals, equal-size near and far, clean cube-like forms; game and infographic look.
options.motion: Objects slide along the iso axes, stack and assemble, extrude upward from the grid; camera pans across the plane without perspective change.
options.use: Tech and SaaS explainers, infrastructure and data-flow diagrams, city and system overviews, infographics.
options.conveys: Systematic clarity, overview, constructed order, a model-world feel.
options.vs: Strictly, isometric uses equal axes; dimetric and trimetric use unequal ones, and pixel-art 'isometric' is really 2:1 dimetric. Orthographic 3D renders real models with a parallel camera, which can include isometric views. Perspective has vanishing points.
options.prompt: Draw the world on an isometric grid: horizontal edges at +30 and -30 degrees, verticals vertical, no vanishing points and no size change with distance. Shade the three visible faces of each block consistently (top lightest, left mid, right darkest, 10-15% value steps). Animate along iso axes only (translate along the 30-degree diagonals or straight up) and build objects by extruding up from the grid.

options.what: Flat 2D shapes or letters given apparent thickness by adding a solid side extrusion behind them.
options.looks: Bold letters and shapes with a visible side depth in a darker shade, often at a 45-degree angle; retro sign or modern chunky-3D look.
options.motion: Extrusion depth grows from zero as a reveal, extrusion angle swings as the shape rotates, pushes compress the depth on impact.
options.use: Headlines and logo reveals, playful and retro brand motion, social content, neo-brutalist graphics.
options.vs: True 3D type has real geometry and lighting; extruded 2D fakes thickness with stacked copies or a long shadow. Long shadow (shadow dimension) fades out and falls to one side; extrusion is a solid body.
options.prompt: Give flat shapes and type an extrusion: 12-24 stacked copies behind the face (or layered text-shadow 1px, 2px ... 16px) offset along a fixed 45-degree direction, filled with a side color 25-35% darker than the face. Reveal by tweening extrusion depth from 0 to full over 400ms (power3.out). Keep the extrusion direction constant across all elements.

options.what: Real 3D objects (devices, products, icons) combined with flat 2D interface, type and graphics in the same frame.
options.looks: A rendered phone, product or 3D icon with lighting and shadow, surrounded or overlaid by flat UI cards, labels and type.
options.motion: The 3D object rotates or floats with physical lighting while the 2D UI animates with standard UI motion; handoffs where a screen on the device becomes the flat UI.
options.use: Hardware and app launch films, product pages, feature reveals with a hero device, 3D icon plus UI explainers.
options.conveys: Premium product reality combined with interface clarity.
options.vs: Full 3D environment puts everything in 3D; this hybrid keeps UI and type flat for legibility. Device-bound UI (UI treatment) concerns framing; this is about dimensional construction.
options.prompt: Combine one lit 3D hero object (Three.js scene, pre-rendered image sequence or high-res render with a baked turntable) with strictly flat 2D UI, labels and type composited on top in HTML/CSS. The 3D object carries lighting, shadow and slow rotation (15-30 degrees over 3s, power2.inOut); flat elements carry no perspective and animate with UI easing. Match the 3D object's accent color to the UI accent.

options.what: A complete three-dimensional world, with modeled objects, lighting and space, explored by a virtual camera.
options.looks: Lit scenes with volume, floors, horizons, cast shadows and reflections; every object valid from any angle.
options.motion: Free camera moves (dolly, orbit, crane, fly-through), physically lit objects, depth of field and atmosphere.
options.use: Brand films, abstract 3D motion, product worlds, game-like explainers, event openers.
options.vs: 2.5D uses flat layers in depth and breaks if the camera orbits; a full 3D environment survives any camera move. Deep cinematic environment is a full 3D environment with cinematic scale, atmosphere and lensing.
options.prompt: Build the world in real 3D: a Three.js scene with modeled geometry, a key light plus fill and a soft environment map, ground plane with contact shadows, and a perspective camera (35-50mm equivalent). Drive camera and object animation from the paused GSAP timeline (seek-safe; no requestAnimationFrame clock). Keep type and UI as HTML overlays unless they must live in the world. If WebGL is out of scope, use pre-rendered footage.

options.what: Real 3D models rendered through a camera with no perspective, so parallel lines stay parallel and size does not change with distance.
options.looks: Clean diagrammatic 3D, often isometric-like angles; lit and shaded volumes but no foreshortening; toy-model or blueprint feeling.
options.motion: Objects rotate on turntables and assemble; camera orbits change the angle without perspective distortion; zoom changes scale uniformly.
options.use: Technical and system explainers, product exploded views, isometric-style SaaS illustrations with real lighting.
options.vs: Isometric (drawn) is pseudo-3D and fixed to one angle; orthographic 3D uses real models and can rotate freely. Perspective 3D adds vanishing points and foreshortening.
options.prompt: Render real 3D models through an orthographic camera (Three.js OrthographicCamera) at an isometric-style angle (azimuth 45 degrees, elevation about 35 degrees), soft key light and ambient occlusion, no perspective or depth blur. Animate assembly and exploded views along the model's axes; orbit the camera 30-90 degrees for angle changes; zoom by changing camera zoom, not distance.

options.what: 3D rendered through a perspective camera with vanishing points, foreshortening and size change with distance.
options.looks: Natural, photographic spatial feel: near things large, far things small, converging lines; lens choice (wide vs long) shapes the drama.
options.motion: Dollies and push-ins change perspective as well as size; orbits reveal form; wide lenses exaggerate speed and depth, long lenses compress it.
options.use: Product hero shots, 3D brand films, spatial UI, cinematic explainers.
options.vs: Orthographic 3D has no foreshortening; pseudo-3D card tilts use CSS perspective on flat planes, which is perspective without volume.
options.prompt: Render 3D with a perspective camera; choose the lens deliberately: 24-28mm equivalent (FOV about 65-75 degrees) for dramatic depth and speed, 50mm (about 40 degrees) for natural, 85mm+ (under 25 degrees) for compressed, product-like calm. Keep the horizon level unless tilting is intentional. Camera moves are dollies (moving the camera), not FOV zooms, so perspective shifts.

options.what: Flat interface panels floating and arranged in a 3D space around the viewer, often with depth, glass and light.
options.looks: Translucent windows at different distances and angles, soft shadows and glow, depth of field, sometimes a real or blurred environment behind; visionOS and sci-fi UI heritage.
options.motion: Panels drift into position in depth, turn to face the viewer, the camera glides between panels; hover lifts toward the viewer.
options.use: XR and spatial computing product films, futuristic UI showcases, AI and productivity concept films.
options.conveys: The future of computing, immersion, sophistication.
options.vs: 2.5D is the construction technique (flat layers in depth) that spatial interfaces usually use; spatial interface is the subject: UI occupying a room. Futuristic UI/FUI is a visual style that may be flat.
options.prompt: Arrange 3-6 UI panels in a perspective container (perspective 1600px, preserve-3d) at depths of -600 to 0px and yaw angles of up to plus or minus 25 degrees, curving around the viewer. Panels use frosted glass (backdrop-filter blur 20px, 1px light border), panels farther away get 2-6px depth blur. Move the camera container slowly between panels (1.5-2.5s, power2.inOut); focused panels ease forward 60-100px on z.

options.what: A vast, atmospheric 3D space with cinematic lensing: fog, volumetric light, deep horizons and strong depth of field.
options.looks: Huge scale, layers of haze receding to a horizon, god rays, silhouettes, shallow focus on a hero object; film-like color grade.
options.motion: Slow, heavy camera moves (long dollies, cranes, reveals), atmospheric particles drifting, rack focus between planes.
options.use: Brand manifesto films, trailers and title sequences, event openers, high-end product launches.
options.vs: Full 3D environment can be clean and diagrammatic; a deep cinematic environment adds atmosphere, lensing and grade. 2.5D can fake it with layered matte paintings.
options.prompt: Build a deep cinematic space: 5+ depth planes (or a Three.js scene with exponential fog), strong atmospheric perspective (distant planes 30-50% lighter and desaturated into the fog color), one volumetric light shaft (a soft gradient beam, screen blend, 15-25%), drifting dust particles, and shallow focus on the hero. Camera moves are slow and long (4-8s dollies or cranes, power1.inOut). In 2D, fake it with 2.5D layers plus haze gradients.
